mainTopic: Visiting a sick person when there is a נדר of הנאה between the visitor and the sick person: why the visitor may stand but not sit (the גמרא on the משנה in נדרים 38b–39a)
overview: The משנה taught that if one person is forbidden by a נדר to benefit from another, he may still visit him when he is sick, standing but not sitting. The גמרא asks which direction the נדר goes, since either direction seems to clash with that rule. שמואל says the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person, in a place where people are paid for sitting with the sick. When asked why the rule is stated so flatly, the גמרא gives two answers: payment properly belongs only to sitting, or there is a גזירה against lingering. עולא says the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor, but the vow left out what the sick person needs for his own life, and a standing visit is enough. A ברייתא lets the visitor go in when the man himself is sick, but only ask in the market when his son is sick. This fits עולא, and שמואל answers that the ברייתא is the opposite case from the משנה. The גמרא then asks what justifies that flat split, and רבא's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Which Direction Does the Vow Go?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the משנה is talking about, and shows that both possible directions of the נדר seem to clash with the rule of 'standing but not sitting'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with? If the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person, he should be allowed to sit too! If the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor, he should not even be allowed to stand!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which person in the משנה is forbidden to benefit from the other. It shows that each choice makes the משנה's rule of 'stand but don't sit' hard to understand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the visitor's things are forbidden to the sick person, the visitor gives nothing of his own by visiting, so even sitting should be fine. If the sick person's things are forbidden to the visitor, then just entering his house is already benefit, so even standing should be forbidden. Neither choice explains the middle position of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing?
The property of
The visitor (of a sick person)
A sick person
Forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: Keep track of the two directions. 'נכסי מבקר אסורין על חולה' means the sick person may not benefit from the VISITOR. 'נכסי חולה אסורין על המבקר' means the visitor may not benefit from the SICK PERSON. The whole סוגיא depends on which one we mean.

phrases.english: GEMARA: With what case are we dealing?

phrases.aramaic: אִי בְּשֶׁנִּכְסֵי מְבַקֵּר אֲסוּרִין עַל חוֹלֶה
phrases.english: If it is where the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person,
then even sitting should also be allowed!

phrases.aramaic: אִי בְּשֶׁנִּכְסֵי חוֹלֶה אֲסוּרִין עַל הַמְבַקֵּר
phrases.english: If it is where the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor,
then even standing should also not be allowed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה that allows the visitor to stand but not sit.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which direction does the נדר go in the משנה's case, so that standing is allowed but sitting is not?

steps.title: שמואל: The Visitor's Property Is Forbidden, and Sitting Is Paid Work
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person, and the case is a place where people are paid for sitting with the sick but not for standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: Really, the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person. The case is in a place where people take payment for sitting with the sick, but not for standing.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל picks the first option: the sick person may not benefit from the visitor. He explains the standing/sitting split by the local custom about payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Where people are paid to sit with the sick, a visitor who sits for free is giving the sick person something worth money. That is forbidden benefit. Standing is not paid work there, so a standing visit gives no forbidden benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually (keeping the first option)
Payment, wages
Sitting (with the sick person)
Standing

phrases.english: שמואל said:

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם בְּשֶׁנִּכְסֵי מְבַקֵּר אֲסוּרִין עַל הַחוֹלֶה,
phrases.english: Really, it is where the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person,
and it is in a place where people take payment for sitting,
and they do not take payment for standing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1 by choosing the first direction and adding a local-custom condition.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person; sitting is forbidden only because, where sitting is paid, a free sit gives the sick person something worth money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A visitor whose property is forbidden to the sick person may stand but not sit, in a place where sitting with the sick is paid.

steps.title: Why Is the Rule Stated So Flatly?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה gives a flat rule of standing versus sitting, when according to שמואל it depends on local custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is it stated as a fixed rule?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל: if everything depends on a local payment custom, why does the משנה state 'standing, not sitting' as a fixed rule? This sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If people were paid for standing too, standing would also be forbidden. The משנה's flat wording suggests something built into sitting versus standing, not just a local habit.

keyTerms.meaning: Why is it stated as a fixed, unqualified rule?

phrases.english: Why is it stated as a fixed rule?
phrases.notes: He means: why does the משנה split sitting and standing so neatly, as if it is always that way?

steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's reading that the standing/sitting split depends on a local payment custom.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rule that depends on custom should not be written as a fixed, unqualified split between standing and sitting.

steps.title: Proper Practice Is Payment Only for Sitting
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה teaches the correct practice: even where payment is taken, it should be for sitting and not for standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us this: even in a place where people take payment, for sitting one should take payment, but for standing one should not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה's flat rule reflects how things should properly be done everywhere that payment is taken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wherever payment for visiting exists, it is proper to charge only for sitting, never for standing. So the split is not a random local habit but the right standard, and that is why the משנה can state it flatly.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us
One should take (payment)

phrases.english: It teaches us this:
that even in a place where people take payment,
for sitting, one should take payment,
for standing, one should not take payment.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּאַף בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁנּוֹטְלִין שָׂכָר
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the flat wording as teaching a proper standard of practice.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The split looked like a mere local custom that could easily vary.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה teaches that wherever payment is taken, it properly applies only to sitting, so the split is fixed.

steps.title: Second Answer: A Decree in Case He Stays Too Long
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: like the view of רבי שמעון בן אליקים, sitting is forbidden by a גזירה, out of concern that the visitor will stay too long.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it is like רבי שמעון בן אליקים, who made a decree in case he lingers while standing. Here too there is a decree in case he lingers while sitting.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different reason for the fixed rule. It compares the case to a decree of רבי שמעון בן אליקים about lingering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן אליקים forbade something out of concern that a person would linger longer than allowed. In the same way, a sitting visitor tends to stay a long time and may end up giving real benefit, so the חכמים forbade sitting altogether. That makes the rule fixed and not dependent on local custom.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another answer)
A rabbinic decree made as a protective fence
In case he lingers / stays too long

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
it is like רבי שמעון בן אליקים,
phrases.notes: His ruling is about a different case, quoted elsewhere in this מסכת; the גמרא borrows only his reasoning here.

phrases.english: a decree in case he lingers while standing.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי גְּזֵירָה שֶׁמָּא יִשְׁהֶא בִּישִׁיבָה.
phrases.english: Here too, a decree in case he lingers while sitting.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: כִּדְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְיָקִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, independent answer to the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the fixed rule as a protective גזירה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Sitting seemed forbidden only because of local payment habits.
steps.terutzMaskana: Sitting is always forbidden by a גזירה, out of concern that the visitor will linger and give real benefit.
steps.whatToRemember: According to שמואל, the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person. Sitting is forbidden either because it is the proper paid service, or because of a גזירה against lingering.

steps.title: עולא: The Sick Person's Property Is Forbidden, but Not for His Own Life
steps.stepSummary: עולא says the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor, but the sick person's נדר did not include what is needed for his own life.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: Really, the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor, and the case is where he did not include in his vow things needed for his life.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא answers the opening question the other way: the visitor may not benefit from the sick person. He adds that the vow left out anything connected to the sick person's own life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A visit helps the sick person, so we assume he never meant his vow to block visits that help keep him alive. That is why entering is allowed even though it uses his house.

keyTerms.meaning: He made him vow / he forbade by vow
His life, what he needs to live

phrases.english: עולא said:

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם בְּשֶׁנִּכְסֵי חוֹלֶה אֲסוּרִין עַל הַמְבַקֵּר,
phrases.english: Really, it is where the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor,
and where he did not include in the vow things needed for his life.
phrases.notes: "His life" means the sick person's own well-being, which a visit helps.

steps.triggerLanguage: עוּלָּא אָמַר: לְעוֹלָם בְּשֶׁנִּכְסֵי חוֹלֶה אֲסוּרִין עַל הַמְבַקֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the opening question of step 1 and answers with the second direction, unlike שמואל.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor, but the vow did not cover what serves the sick person's own life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A visit that serves the sick person's life is outside the vow, so entering is allowed.

steps.title: Then Sitting Should Be Allowed Too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges עולא: if life needs are outside the vow, sitting should be allowed too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even sitting should be allowed too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on עולא: if visits for the sick person's life are outside the vow, why stop the visitor from sitting?
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא's exception seems to cover the whole visit. Nothing he said explains why standing is allowed but sitting is not.

keyTerms.meaning: If so

phrases.english: If so, even sitting should be allowed too!

steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's exception for the sick person's life needs.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the visit is excluded from the vow, the exclusion should include sitting as well as standing.

steps.title: Standing Is Enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the visit can be done while standing, so sitting is not needed for the sick person's life.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is possible to do it standing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends עולא: the exception covers only what is truly needed, and a standing visit is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vow left out only what the sick person's life really needs. Since a standing visit does the job, sitting is extra and stays under the vow.

keyTerms.meaning: Possible

phrases.english: But it is possible to do it standing!

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the exception to what is truly necessary.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The life-needs exception seemed to cover the whole visit, including sitting.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only what is necessary is excluded; standing is enough, so sitting stays forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: According to עולא, the visitor may not benefit from the sick person, but a standing visit is allowed because the vow never covered what the sick person needs for his life.

steps.title: A ברייתא: He Visits the Man, but Asks About the Son in the Market
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: if the man himself is sick, the visitor may come in; if his son is sick, he may only ask about him in the market.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: If he became sick, he goes in to visit him. If his son became sick, he asks about him in the market.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to test the two opinions. This is a setup; next the גמרא will check which opinion the ברייתא fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא treats the man and his son differently. The visitor may enter for the man but not for the son. Any explanation of the vow has to account for that difference.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged (from a ברייתא)
He asks about him in the market (without entering the house)

phrases.english: They challenged from a ברייתא:
If he himself became sick, he goes in to visit him;
if his son became sick, he asks about him in the market.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an outside source to test both שמואל and עולא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two explanations of the משנה, especially שמואל's (as the next lines will show).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lets the visitor enter for the man but not for his son, and any explanation must account for that difference.

steps.title: The ברייתא Fits עולא Well
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the ברייתא fits עולא: the vow left out only the sick man's own life needs, not his son's.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for עולא, who said the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor and the vow did not include things needed for his life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the ברייתא fits nicely with עולא. This prepares the next move, where it will ask how שמואל can explain it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For עולא, the sick man left his own life needs out of the vow. A visit to the man serves his own life, so the visitor may come in. The son's illness is not the man's own life, so the vow still forbids entering his house, and the visitor must ask in the market.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well for (one side; a 'but' about the other side usually follows)
Fine, it fits well

steps.confusionAlert: 'בשלמא' means only one side has been checked. The גמרא is about to ask how the ברייתא fits the OTHER opinion (שמואל), so this is not the end of the discussion.

phrases.english: It works well for עולא, who said
it is where the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor,

phrases.aramaic: וּכְגוֹן דְּלָא אַדְּרֵיהּ מִן חַיּוּתֵיהּ — שַׁפִּיר.
phrases.english: and where he did not include in the vow things needed for his life: that fits well.
phrases.notes: The exception covered the man's own life, not his son's, so the visitor may not go in for the son.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Checks the ברייתא from step 9 against עולא first, setting up the challenge to שמואל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא distinguishing the sick man (visitor may enter) from his sick son (visitor asks in the market).

steps.title: How would שמואל explain the father/son difference?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: if the case is that the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person, why should it matter whether the father or the son is sick?
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to שמואל, who said the case is where the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person, what is the difference between him and his son?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to שמואל and asks how he could explain the ברייתא that treats a sick father differently from a sick son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For עולא the difference made sense: the vow did not include the sick man's own life needs, but it did include his son's. In שמואל's case the forbidden property belongs to the visitor, not the sick person. So that reason does not work, and nothing seems to separate a sick father from a sick son.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference? A challenge asking why two cases are treated differently.
The visitor (the one coming to visit the sick person).
The sick person.
Property, belongings.

phrases.english: But according to שמואל,
who said: it is where the visitor's property
is forbidden to the sick person,

phrases.aramaic: מַאי שְׁנָא הוּא וּמַאי שְׁנָא בְּנוֹ?
phrases.english: what is different about him and what is different about his son?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After showing the ברייתא fits עולא, the גמרא tests whether it can also fit שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's reading of the משנה (visitor's property forbidden to the sick person).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's father/son split only makes sense when the sick person's property is forbidden. In שמואל's case there is no reason for the split.

steps.title: The משנה and the ברייתא are opposite cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers on שמואל's behalf that the משנה is about the visitor's property being forbidden to the sick person, while the ברייתא is about the sick person's property being forbidden to the visitor.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל could say to you: the משנה is where the visitor's property is forbidden to the sick person. The ברייתא is where the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for שמואל: the ברייתא is not talking about his case at all. It is talking about the opposite case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל keeps his reading of the משנה but splits the two sources. The ברייתא is about the sick person's property being forbidden, which is the same as עולא's case. So the father/son difference can be explained the same way as in step 10, and the challenge goes away.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you. The גמרא answering on behalf of an אמורא.
Our משנה.
A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה.

steps.confusionAlert: Watch which property is forbidden to whom. In the משנה (for שמואל) it is the visitor's property that is forbidden to the sick person. In the ברייתא it is the reverse: the sick person's property is forbidden to the visitor.

phrases.english: He could say to you:
The משנה is where the visitor's property
is forbidden to the sick person;
the ברייתא is where the sick person's property
is forbidden to the visitor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 11 by saying the ברייתא deals with a different case than the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separating the cases: the two sources are about opposite situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was thought to be about the same case as the משנה, which would clash with שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about the sick person's property being forbidden to the visitor, so it does not clash with שמואל's reading of the משנה.
steps.whatToRemember: Both עולא and שמואל can explain the ברייתא. For שמואל, the משנה and the ברייתא are simply opposite cases.

steps.title: Why split the משנה and the ברייתא so flatly?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we can assign the משנה and the ברייתא to opposite cases without any qualification, and רבא begins to answer by explaining שמואל's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: What made it so clear-cut? רבא said: שמואל...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer it just gave: how can we be so sure which case each source is talking about? It then sets up רבא's answer, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither the משנה nor the ברייתא says outright whose property is forbidden. So the גמרא wants to know what justifies the flat split. Here רבא only begins his answer by naming שמואל; his actual explanation comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: What makes it clear-cut? Asking why something is stated as a flat, unqualified rule.
An אמורא who now begins answering the question.

phrases.english: Why was it stated so flatly?
phrases.notes: He means: how do we know for sure that the משנה is one case and the ברייתא is the other?

phrases.english: Rava said: As for Shmuel...
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; without it, רבא is explaining שמואל's view, not quoting him. His sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the basis for the split given in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What justifies assigning the משנה and the ברייתא to opposite cases without qualification?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבא begins an answer explaining שמואל's view; his explanation continues on the next amud.
